claim: Agents asked to grade their own work skew positive even when quality is mediocre, so a separate evaluator agent is a strong lever, but separation alone does not remove the leniency because the evaluator is still an LLM that favors LLM-written output.
why: In the author's experiments, tuning a standalone evaluator to be skeptical was more tractable than making the generator critical of its own work, and it gave the generator concrete feedback to act on.
check: Check whether a generator is grading its own work and whether a separate evaluator, if used, has been tuned to challenge the kinds of outputs it previously approved too readily.
quote: agents reliably skew positive when grading their own work

claim: On the Opus 4.5 harness, out-of-the-box Claude was a poor QA agent: it found real issues and then talked itself into approving the work, and it tested superficially without probing edge cases.
why: Getting a useful evaluator took several rounds of reading its logs, finding where its judgment diverged from the author's, and updating its prompt, and even then undiscovered bugs remained in deeper features.
check: Check QA logs for early approvals that overlook real defects or skip edge cases, and look for prompt revisions that address those failures.
quote: Out of the box, Claude is a poor QA agent. In early runs, I watched it identify legitimate issues, then talk itself into deciding they weren't a big deal and approve the work anyway.

claim: In the frontend design experiment, the author calibrated the evaluator with few-shot examples containing detailed score breakdowns, aligning its judgment with the author's preferences and reducing score drift across iterations.
why: The worked score breakdowns showed the evaluator how the author applied the design criteria.
check: If a frontend design evaluator drifts between iterations or grades differently from the intended rubric, check whether its examples show detailed score breakdowns.
quote: I calibrated the evaluator using few-shot examples with detailed score breakdowns. This ensured the evaluator’s judgment aligned with my preferences, and reduced score drift across iterations.

claim: Each evaluator criterion had a hard threshold, and if any single criterion fell below it the sprint failed and the generator received detailed feedback on what went wrong.
why: A per-criterion pass bar prevents a strong score on one dimension from masking a failure on another, and the failure carries actionable detail back to the generator.
check: If the QA loop is meant to enforce individual pass thresholds, check that any below-threshold criterion fails the sprint and produces detailed feedback for the generator.
quote: Each criterion had a hard threshold, and if any one fell below it, the sprint failed and the generator got detailed feedback on what went wrong.

claim: Before each sprint the generator proposed what it would build and how success would be verified, and the evaluator reviewed and negotiated that sprint contract until both agreed on what done meant, before any code was written.
why: The product spec was intentionally high-level, so the contract bridged user stories to testable behavior; contracts were granular (sprint 3 alone had 27 criteria) and the evaluator graded against them.
check: In a process that composes a contract and then runs an executor, check that the reviewer grades against that same contract and that the contract holds testable criteria; vague 'done' wording is a finding.
quote: Before each sprint, the generator and evaluator negotiated a sprint contract: agreeing on what "done" looked like for that chunk of work before any code was written.

claim: In the updated long-running app harness, the author kept the planner that turned a 1-4 sentence prompt into a full spec because without it the generator started building before scoping the work and produced a less feature-rich app.
why: Given only the raw prompt the generator started building without speccing its work.
check: When a short prompt is the only input, check whether dropping the planner causes the generator to skip scoping and deliver fewer features than intended.
quote: Without the planner, the generator under-scoped: given the raw prompt, it would start building without first speccing its work, and end up creating a less feature-rich application than the planner did.

claim: The planner was told to stay at product context and high-level technical design rather than granular implementation, and to constrain deliverables while letting the executor find the path.
why: If the planner specified granular technical details and got one wrong, the error would cascade into the downstream implementation.
check: Check whether the planner commits the executor to granular technical choices that could propagate a planning error into implementation.
quote: I prompted it to be ambitious about scope and to stay focused on product context and high level technical design rather than detailed technical implementation.

claim: In Anthropic's app builds with Opus 4.5 and 4.6, a separate evaluator earned its cost when tasks stretched what the generator could reliably do on its own.
why: The evaluator caught meaningful issues across the Opus 4.5 builds, became overhead on tasks Opus 4.6 could handle solo, and still helped on Opus 4.6 tasks near its limits.
check: Check whether the evaluator still catches important issues on this task that the current generator misses on its own.
quote: The practical implication is that the evaluator is not a fixed yes-or-no decision. It is worth the cost when the task sits beyond what the current model does reliably solo.

claim: In Anthropic's earlier long-task tests, Claude Sonnet 4.5 began wrapping up prematurely as it approached what it believed was its context limit, and compaction alone fell short, so the harness used resets with structured handoffs.
why: Compaction keeps continuity but gives no clean slate so the anxiety can persist, whereas a reset gives a clean slate at the cost of a handoff artifact that must carry enough state; resets add orchestration complexity, token overhead and latency.
check: If a harness resets context between sessions, check which model it was built for and whether the reset logic is still needed on the current model (see the Opus 4.5 claim from the same source).
quote: In our earlier testing, we found Claude Sonnet 4.5 exhibited context anxiety strongly enough that compaction alone wasn't sufficient to enable strong long task performance, so context resets became essential to the harness design.

claim: Opus 4.5 largely removed the context-anxiety behavior on its own, so the author dropped context resets and ran the whole build as one continuous session with the Agent SDK's automatic compaction.
why: For this build, automatic compaction handled context growth in one continuous session after Opus 4.5 largely removed the premature wrap-up behavior.
check: If a harness used resets to address Sonnet 4.5's context anxiety, check whether an Opus 4.5 run can sustain the same work with automatic compaction alone.
quote: Opus 4.5 largely removed that behavior on its own, so I was able to drop context resets from this harness entirely.

claim: After Opus 4.6 shipped, the author removed sprint decomposition, kept the planner and evaluator, and moved evaluation from each sprint to the end of the build.
why: Opus 4.6 plans more carefully and sustains agentic tasks longer, so the builder ran coherently for over two hours without sprints that Opus 4.5 had needed.
check: When upgrading a sprint-based build harness, check whether the new model can sustain the build without sprint decomposition and whether QA can move to the end of the build.
quote: I moved the evaluator to a single pass at the end of the run rather than grading per sprint.

claim: The first attempt to simplify the harness by cutting it back radically and adding new ideas failed to match the original and left it unclear which pieces were load-bearing, so the author switched to removing one component at a time and reviewing the effect on the final result.
why: Every component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do alone, and those assumptions may be wrong or go stale as models improve.
check: If a simplification regresses the result and changes several components at once, check whether testing removals individually would show which components the harness still needs.
quote: I moved to a more methodical approach, removing one component at a time and reviewing what impact it had on the final result.

claim: Every harness component encodes an assumption about what the model cannot do on its own, those assumptions should be stress-tested, and when a new model lands the harness should be re-examined by stripping pieces no longer load-bearing and adding pieces for new capability.
why: The assumptions can be incorrect and can quickly go stale as models improve; the post ties this to the principle of the simplest solution that works.
check: For each component kept after a model upgrade, check which limitation it addresses and whether that limitation still affects performance with the new model.
quote: every component in a harness encodes an assumption about what the model can't do on its own, and those assumptions are worth stress testing, both because they may be incorrect, and because they can quickly go stale as models improve.

claim: On Opus 4.5 the full planner-generator-evaluator harness took 6 hours and $200 against 20 minutes and $9 for a solo agent on the same retro game-maker prompt, over 20x the cost, and the solo run's core feature (entities responding to input) was broken while the harness run's worked.
why: The comparison used the same prompt and showed a difference in the core play mode, although the full harness output still had rough edges.
check: For a comparable build, check whether the added cost buys a measurable improvement on core features against a solo run of the same task.
quote: The harness was over 20x more expensive, but the difference in output quality was immediately apparent.

claim: In the simplified harness (built after Opus 4.6 shipped) a DAW build took 3 hr 50 min and $124.70 in total, with the planner costing $0.46 and QA run in three rounds of 6.8 to 9.6 minutes each; the source's per-round table shows the builder rounds as the bulk of the cost.
why: The reported builder rounds accounted for most of the time and token cost in that run.
check: When assessing the cost of a similar build loop, compare the measured QA and builder costs for that run before attributing the overhead to review.
quote:
QA (Round 2)

6.8 min

$3.09

Build (Round 3)

10.9 min

$5.88

QA (Round 3)

9.6 min

$4.06

Total V2 Harness

3 hr 50 min

$124.70

claim: In the updated harness's three-round DAW build, QA found display-only core features in its first round and reported stub-only audio recording and missing clip resize and split in its second round.
why: The first QA report found that several interactions explicitly required by the spec were missing even though the app looked impressive and its AI integration worked.
check: Check whether QA exercises the spec's core interactions in the running app so that a display-only or stub feature cannot pass as complete.
quote:
In its second round feedback, it again caught several functionality gaps:

Remaining gaps:
- Audio recording is still stub-only (button toggles but no mic capture)
- Clip resize by edge drag and clip split not implemented
- Effect visualizations are numeric sliders, not graphical (no EQ curve)

claim: In the frontend design loop the evaluator drove the live page with the Playwright MCP before scoring each criterion, the loop ran 5 to 15 iterations, and full runs took up to four hours because each cycle took real wall-clock time.
why: Navigating the page rather than scoring a static screenshot gave grounded critiques but made every cycle slow.
check: For a similar design loop, check how much wall-clock time each round of live-page evaluation adds when estimating the cost of multiple iterations.
quote: I ran 5 to 15 iterations per generation, with each iteration typically pushing the generator in a more distinctive direction as it responded to the evaluator's critique. Because the evaluator was actively navigating the page rather than scoring a static screenshot, each cycle took real wall-clock time. Full runs stretched up to four hours.

claim: In the frontend design experiment, scores generally improved unevenly, later implementations tended to be better as a whole, the author regularly preferred a middle iteration to the last one, and complexity tended to grow each round.
why: The evaluator's assessments improved over iterations before plateauing with headroom remaining, so more rounds did not guarantee better output.
check: Check whether a design loop that returns its last iteration compares that output with earlier candidates before treating another round as an improvement.
quote: While scores generally improved over iterations, the pattern was not always cleanly linear. Later implementations tended to be better as a whole, but I regularly saw cases where I preferred a middle iteration over the last one.

claim: In the Opus 4.6 C compiler experiment, an agent locked a task by writing a text file to `current_tasks/`.
why: Git synchronization made the second agent pick a different task if two agents tried to claim the same work.
check: For independently claimable tasks, check whether the team has a way to detect duplicate claims and send the second worker to another task.
quote: Claude takes a "lock" on a task by writing a text file to current_tasks/ (e.g., one agent might lock current_tasks/parse_if_statement.txt, while another locks current_tasks/codegen_function_definition.txt). If two agents try to claim the same task, git's synchronization forces the second agent to pick a different one.

claim: The C compiler project with Opus 4.6 ran nearly 2,000 Claude Code sessions over two weeks, consumed 2 billion input tokens and 140 million output tokens, and cost just under $20,000.
why: The author calls it extremely expensive against a Max plan but a fraction of what a human team would cost; it was designed as a capability benchmark.
check: When budgeting a comparable compiler-scale multi-agent run, check the expected session and token volumes against the reported run and the project's own limits.
quote: Over nearly 2,000 Claude Code sessions across two weeks, Opus 4.6 consumed 2 billion input tokens and generated 140 million output tokens, a total cost just under $20,000.

claim: The compiler experiment's author says an autonomous loop needs a nearly perfect task verifier to keep Claude from solving the wrong problem, and added stricter CI checks after new features started breaking existing functionality.
why: Claude had started frequently breaking existing functionality with each new feature.
check: Check whether the loop's verifier matches the task and whether its checks catch regressions in existing functionality before changes are accepted.
quote: that the task verifier is nearly perfect, otherwise Claude will solve the wrong problem.

claim: For agent-facing tests, the compiler experiment's author recommends short console output, detailed logs with one-line ERROR reasons and precomputed summaries, and used a default `--fast` option with a 1% or 10% sample that was deterministic per agent.
why: Verbose output fills context, and the author observed that Claude can spend hours running tests unless the harness helps it manage that work.
check: Check whether agent-facing test output hides the useful result in verbose logs or whether repeated test runs dominate work that a deterministic fast sample could support.
quote: The test harness should not print thousands of useless bytes. At most, it should print a few lines of output and log all important information to a file so Claude can find it when needed.

claim: In the Opus 4.6 compiler experiment, agents picked different independent failing tests, but all 16 hit the same Linux-kernel compilation bug and overwrote one another's fixes until a GCC oracle helped them isolate different files.
why: The fix was a test harness that compiled most of the kernel with GCC and only a random subset with Claude's compiler, so each agent could isolate different bugs.
check: Before parallelizing a coupled debugging task, check whether workers can isolate different failures instead of repeatedly fixing the same one.
quote: Unlike a test suite with hundreds of independent tests, compiling the Linux kernel is one giant task. Every agent would hit the same bug, fix that bug, and then overwrite each other's changes. Having 16 agents running didn't help because each was stuck solving the same task.

claim: In the long-lived parallel team the author also ran standing specialist agents (deduplicating code, compiler performance, efficiency of emitted code, design critique, documentation) beside the agents solving the problem.
why: The author assigned deduplication to a specialist because LLM-written code frequently reimplemented functionality that already existed.
check: When a parallel compiler team repeatedly reimplements functionality, check who is responsible for finding and coalescing duplicate code.
quote: LLM-written code frequently re-implements existing functionality, so I tasked one agent with coalescing any duplicate code it found.

claim: Near the limits of Opus 4.6 in the compiler experiment, new features and bug fixes frequently broke existing functionality, and the author cautions that passing tests can give a false impression that an autonomous run is done.
why: For example, the compiler fell back to GCC for the 16-bit x86 boot phase because its own compiled output exceeded Linux's size limit.
check: Check whether a passing suite conceals regressions or unsupported paths that matter to the autonomous compiler run's actual goal.
quote: New features and bugfixes frequently broke existing functionality.

claim: In the compiler harness, where each Claude Code agent started in a fresh container with no context, the prompt instructed agents to maintain extensive READMEs and progress files and update them frequently with current status.
why: Fresh agents on a large project can spend significant time orienting themselves, and the files give them the project's current state before they reach the tests.
check: For loops that spawn fresh executor sessions, check that a progress or state file exists and that the prompt requires updating it.
quote: I included instructions to maintain extensive READMEs and progress files that should be updated frequently with the current status.

claim: Anthropic reverted Claude Code's system-prompt length limits on April 20 after broader ablations showed a 3% drop on one eval for both Opus 4.6 and 4.7.
why: The initial eval set showed no regression, and the drop surfaced only when Anthropic ran more ablations with a broader set.
check: Check whether a proposed prompt length limit was ablated against a broad eval suite before shipping.
quote: As part of this investigation, we ran more ablations (removing lines from the system prompt to understand the impact of each line) using a broader set of evaluations. One of these evaluations showed a 3% drop for both Opus 4.6 and 4.7. We immediately reverted the prompt as part of the April 20 release.

claim: On March 4, Claude Code lowered the default effort for Sonnet 4.6 and Opus 4.6 from high to medium to reduce long waits, reversed the decision on April 7 after user feedback, and reported xhigh for Opus 4.7 and high for all other models at the time of the postmortem.
why: Medium effort gave slightly lower intelligence and significantly lower latency for most tasks in internal testing, but users reported that Claude Code felt less intelligent.
check: Check whether effort is pinned in settings or env vars, and that the pinned value fits the task; defaults have moved in both directions and differ by model.
quote: All users now default to xhigh effort for Opus 4.7, and high effort for all other models.

claim: A context-management bug (clearing prior thinking every turn instead of once, in sessions idle over an hour) passed multiple human and automated code reviews, unit tests, end-to-end tests, automated verification and dogfooding, and took over a week to root-cause.
why: The bug crossed Claude Code context management, the API and extended thinking, and two unrelated experiments made it harder to reproduce, including a display change that suppressed it in most CLI sessions.
check: Check whether test coverage exercises the stale-session boundary across context management, the API and extended thinking, including the turns after an idle session resumes.
quote: The changes it introduced made it past multiple human and automated code reviews, as well as unit tests, end-to-end tests, automated verification, and dogfooding.

claim: When back-testing Code Review against the offending pull requests, Opus 4.7 found the bug when it was given the code repositories needed for complete context, while Opus 4.6 did not, and Anthropic is adding support for additional repositories as context for code reviews.
why: In this back-test, the result depended on the model given the repository context needed to investigate the offending pull requests.
check: When reviewing a change that spans repositories, check that Code Review can access the repositories needed to trace the interaction and test whether the chosen reviewer can find that class of bug.
quote: When provided the code repositories necessary to gather complete context, Opus 4.7 found the bug, while Opus 4.6 didn't. To prevent this from happening again, we are now landing support for additional repositories as context for code reviews.

claim: Anthropic said it would run a broad per-model eval suite for every Claude Code system prompt change.
why: Each model behaves differently, and a verbosity change tuned ahead of the Opus 4.7 release exposed regressions for Opus 4.6 and 4.7 on a broader eval.
check: Check whether each Claude Code system prompt change is evaluated on a broad suite for each model.
quote: We will run a broad suite of per-model evals for every system prompt change to Claude Code, continuing ablations to understand the impact of each line, and we have built new tooling to make prompt changes easier to review and audit.

claim: A deeply coupled pipeline such as a differentiable Boltzmann solver is structurally different from the C compiler's farmed-out work, and the author suggests it suits a single agent working sequentially and spawning subagents as needed rather than many parallel agents.
why: A small numerical error early in the chain shifts everything downstream and debugging means tracing causally through the whole chain; this is the author's judgment ('may be better suited'), not a measured comparison.
check: For a coupled numerical solver, check whether the debugging design lets an agent trace a discrepancy through the entire chain and bisect it against the reference implementation.
quote: which may be better suited to a single agent working sequentially, spawning subagents as needed, and using the reference implementation to bisect discrepancies.

claim: In the scientific computing workflow, a progress file called `CHANGELOG.md` serves as portable long-term memory and can track current status, completed tasks, failed approaches and why they failed, accuracy at key checkpoints and known limitations.
why: Without the failed approaches, successive sessions will re-attempt the same dead ends.
check: Check whether the progress file records failed approaches and why they failed so fresh sessions can avoid repeating them.
quote: The failed approaches are important—without them, successive sessions will re-attempt the same dead ends.

claim: The Ralph loop kicks the agent back into context when it claims completion and asks whether it is really done, with an example capped at --max-iterations 20 and a DONE completion promise, to counter agentic laziness in current models.
why: The pattern gives an agent that stops early another chance to recognize unfinished work and continue, with the example using a completion promise and iteration cap.
check: If a Ralph loop asks an agent to keep working toward a measurable target, check that the target is stated in the prompt and identify the configured iteration cap and completion promise.
quote: the Ralph loop, which is essentially a for loop which kicks the agent back into context when it claims completion

claim: Across four analytical decisions, the 50 analysts using Opus 4.8 at High effort in Claude Code matched their agent's hidden, randomly assigned lean 86% of the time, versus about 50% expected without agent influence.
why: The researchers strengthened the agents' preferences for one task in one field with one model, so the effect may be smaller without explicit instructions to voice a preference.
check: Check whether human approvers form and record their own judgment before seeing an agent's recommendation.
quote: Across the four analytical choices, analysts went with their agent’s lean 86% of the time. If the agent’s input made no difference, we’d expect about 50%.

claim: The authors suggest, as areas for future study rather than tested fixes, that agents make the best case for each option or ask the expert for their own view before offering one, because the agents rarely argued strongly for the option they did not lean toward.
why: With only one side argued well the analysts could adopt the agent's assumptions without working out their own; the authors note this could overwhelm users if applied to every decision.
check: For decisions that depend on judgment and values, check whether the agent's output presents both options or asks first; it is a design suggestion, not a validated control.
quote: Agents could make the best case for each option, or ask experts for their own view before offering one.

claim: On the study's analysis task, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 out of 123 runs with no assigned lean.
why: The authors caution that apparent agreement among separate teams may reflect shared model preferences if all the teams defer to models with those preferences.
check: When several teams reach the same judgment with model assistance, check whether they independently considered the options or deferred to models with a shared preference.
quote: with no lean assigned, Claude Opus 4.8 made the same five choices in 112 out of 123 runs

claim: Anthropic identifies three situations where multiple agents consistently beat a single agent (context pollution degrading performance, tasks that can run in parallel, and specialization improving tool selection or task focus) and says outside them coordination costs typically exceed the benefits.
why: Every added agent is another point of failure, another prompt to maintain and another source of unexpected behavior.
check: For each extra agent, check whether isolating context, running work in parallel, or specializing tools or focus gives a benefit that justifies the coordination cost.
quote: three situations where multiple agents consistently outperform a single agent: when context pollution degrades performance, when tasks can run in parallel, and when specialization improves tool selection or task focus.

claim: Anthropic reports that teams have invested months building elaborate multi-agent architectures only to find that improved prompting on a single agent achieved equivalent results, and says multi-agent systems are often applied where a single agent would perform better.
why: The calculus continues to evolve as models improve.
check: Before accepting a multi-agent design, check whether a single agent with better prompting and tools was tried and measured.
quote: teams invest months building elaborate multi-agent architectures only to discover that improved prompting on a single agent achieved equivalent results.

claim: In Anthropic's testing multi-agent implementations typically use 3-10x more tokens than single-agent approaches for equivalent tasks, because of duplicated context, coordination messages and summarizing results for handoffs, and often take longer overall despite parallelism.
why: Each agent needs its own context, and coordination messages and handoff summaries add tokens and total computation.
check: Compare token use and completion time with a single-agent run on equivalent work before treating parallel execution as cheaper or faster.
quote: In our testing, multi-agent implementations typically use 3-10x more tokens than single-agent approaches for equivalent tasks. This overhead stems from duplicating context across agents, coordination messages between agents, and summarizing results for handoffs.

claim: In one Anthropic experiment with agents specialized by software development role (planner, implementer, tester, reviewer) the subagents spent more tokens on coordination than on actual work, and the post says splitting by problem type creates a telephone game in which each handoff degrades fidelity.
why: The experiment illustrates fidelity lost during handoffs, while the separate long-running app harness reports gains from a planner, generator and evaluator using negotiated contracts and live-app QA.
check: For a chain split by software development role, check whether agents lose task context at handoffs or spend more tokens coordinating than doing the work.
quote: In one experiment with agents specialized by software development role (planner, implementer, tester, reviewer), the subagents spent more tokens on coordination than on actual work.

claim: Divide work by context boundary, not by type of work: an agent handling a feature should also handle its tests because it already has the context, and split only where context can truly be isolated (independent research paths, components with clean interfaces, blackbox verification).
why: Sequential phases of the same work, tightly coupled components and work needing shared state share too much context to split without overhead.
check: Check whether different agents plan, implement and write tests for the same feature even though those phases need the same context.
quote: an agent handling a feature should also handle its tests, because it already possesses the necessary context.

claim: A dedicated verification subagent is one pattern that works consistently across domains because it can black-box-test an artifact against explicit criteria with little context transfer, though more capable orchestrators can increasingly evaluate subagent work directly.
why: It sidesteps the telephone-game cost that makes other role splits expensive.
check: Check whether the verifier can determine that the artifact meets explicit criteria using its test tools without needing the full implementation history.
quote: Verification requires minimal context transfer by nature, so a verifier can blackbox-test a system without needing the full history of how it was built.

claim: The post calls premature success after one or two passing tests the most significant failure mode for verification subagents and recommends explicit full-suite instructions, concrete criteria, edge cases and negative tests.
why: The post says verification agents take shortcuts without explicit requirements for comprehensive validation.
check: Check the reviewer prompt for a concrete requirement to run everything and to try inputs that should fail; 'make sure it works' is a finding.
quote: The verifier runs one or two tests, observes them pass, and declares success.

claim: Anthropic says more capable orchestrators such as Claude Opus 4.5 are increasingly able to evaluate subagent work directly without a separate verification step.
why: Direct evaluation avoids transferring implementation context to a separate agent when the orchestrator can assess the work itself.
check: Check whether the current orchestrator can reliably evaluate subagent work directly before removing a separate verification step.
quote: more capable orchestrator models (like Claude Opus 4.5) are increasingly able to evaluate subagent work directly without a separate verification step.

claim: The post's example implement-then-verify loop defaults to 3 attempts, appends the verifier's issues to the requirements on failure, and raises an error if all attempts fail.
why: This is illustrative example code, not a stated recommendation of 3 and not tied to measured results.
check: When assessing a loop based on this example, check that it passes verifier findings to the next attempt and reports failure when the configured attempt limit is reached.
quote:
requirements += f"\n\nPrevious attempt failed: {verification['issues']}"

 raise Exception(f"Failed verification after {max_attempts} attempts")

claim: When an agent has 15-20+ tools, the post suggests considering Tool Search before splitting it, because on-demand discovery can reduce token use by up to 85% while improving tool selection accuracy.
why: The post lists too many tools (often 20+), unrelated domains and degraded performance when adding tools as signals for tool-set specialization, but offers tool search as the cheaper first step.
check: If a subagent exists only to hold a subset of tools, check whether tool search or on-demand loading would remove the need for it.
quote: Before adopting a multi-agent architecture, consider using the Tool Search Tool, which lets Claude dynamically discover tools on-demand rather than loading all definitions upfront. This can reduce token usage by up to 85% while improving tool selection accuracy.

claim: For parallel exploration of a large search space, the post identifies broader coverage as the primary benefit and says it costs more tokens and often takes longer overall than a single agent.
why: Running the extra work concurrently can be faster than running all of it sequentially, even when doing more total computation makes the multi-agent run slower than a single-agent run.
check: When parallelizing search, compare the coverage, token use and elapsed time with a single-agent run before assuming a speed gain.
quote: The primary benefit of parallelization is thoroughness, not speed.

claim: Context isolation in a subagent is most effective when the subtask generates high context volume (over 1000 tokens) but most of it is irrelevant to the main task, when the subtask is well-defined with clear criteria for what to extract, and for lookup or retrieval that needs filtering before use.
why: In the post's example the main agent receives only the 50-100 tokens it needs instead of 2000+ tokens of order history.
check: For a subagent intended to protect context, check whether it filters a large result down to the information the main agent actually needs.
quote: Context isolation is most effective when subtasks generate high context volume (more than 1000 tokens) but most of that information is irrelevant to the main task

claim: On complex work in one long context, Claude Code can stop after partial progress such as addressing 35 of 50 items, favor its own results during verification, or drift from the goal as compaction can lose edge-case requirements or prohibitions.
why: Dynamic workflows help address these failure modes by giving separate subagents their own contexts and focused goals.
check: When a complex single-context task stops early, favors its own findings, or loses requirements after compaction, check whether separate subagents with focused goals address the observed failure.
quote:
Self-preferential bias refers to Claude’s tendency to prefer its own results or findings, especially when asked to verify or judge them against a rubric.

Goal drift refers to the gradual loss of fidelity to the original objective across many turns, especially after compaction. Each summarization step is lossy, and details like edge-case requirements or "don't do X" constraints can get lost.

claim: For work of unknown size the 'loop until done' pattern keeps spawning agents until a stop condition is met (no new findings, or no more errors in the logs) instead of a fixed number of passes, and the post suggests pairing repeatable workflows with /goal to set a hard completion requirement.
why: When the amount of work is unknown, an observable stop condition lets the workflow continue while it is still finding issues.
check: For a loop with an unknown amount of work, check whether it stops on an observable completion condition such as no new findings or no more errors in the logs.
quote: loop spawning agents until a stop condition is met (no new findings, or no more errors in the logs) instead of a fixed number of passes.

claim: The adversarial verification pattern runs, for each spawned agent, a separate agent that verifies its output against a rubric or criteria, and a skeptic subagent can be added to filter false positives from rule-by-rule verifiers.
why: A separate context helps counter self-preferential bias, and in the rule-review example a skeptic can reduce false positives.
check: Check that adversarial verification uses a separate agent with a rubric, and consider a skeptic when rule-by-rule review produces too many false positives.
quote: For each spawned agent, run a separate spawned agent to adversarially verify its output against a rubric or criteria.

claim: Dynamic workflows can use significantly more tokens, so the post recommends asking whether a regular coding task needs the added compute and notes that most do not need a panel of 5 reviewers.
why: The post says workflows are best for complex, high-value tasks and best practices are still developing; the same judgment applies to the multi-agent versus single-agent decision.
check: If routine coding changes automatically get a reviewer panel, check whether the extra compute is warranted for those tasks.
quote: most traditional coding tasks do not need a panel of 5 reviewers.

claim: For qualitative ranking of a large list in a dynamic workflow, the post suggests pairwise comparison agents or parallel bucket ranking followed by a merge, and says pairwise judgments are more reliable than absolute scores.
why: In the pairwise pattern each comparison gets a fresh agent, so the deterministic loop can keep the running order without putting the full list in one agent's context.
check: If a large qualitative sort is sent to one prompt and strains context or quality, check whether a pairwise workflow would keep comparisons small.
quote: Instead run a tournament, a pipeline of pairwise-comparison agents (comparative judgment is more reliable than absolute scoring), or bucket-rank in parallel then merge. Each comparison is its own agent, so the deterministic loop holds the bracket and only the running order stays in context.

claim: For triage workflows the quarantine pattern bars agents that read untrusted public content from taking high-privilege actions, which are done by a separate acting agent that sees only their summaries.
why: Text read from the outside can be interpreted as instructions, so the reader agent has no privileges to misuse.
check: In a triage workflow, check whether agents that read untrusted public content lack access to the high-privilege actions reserved for the separate acting agent.
quote: barring the agents that read untrusted public content from taking high-privilege actions

claim: A token budget for a dynamic workflow can be set by prompting for it (for example 'use 10k tokens'), which sets the cap.
why: Dynamic workflows can use more tokens, so the cap limits how many tokens the task uses.
check: If a dynamic workflow needs a token cap, check whether its prompt specifies the intended token budget.
quote: You can set explicit token usage budgets for dynamic workflows to limit how many tokens a task uses. You can prompt it with a budget like: “use 10k tokens,” which will set the cap.

claim: In a toy experiment, 1,000 agents on an early Claude Fable 5.2 reproduced the earlier formalization of Fermat's Last Theorem in 28.7 hours, using one-third as many output tokens as the September run.
why: The toy run used neither the Prove2Me platform nor researcher steering, both of which the September run relied on.
check: When estimating the cost of a similar proof run, check whether its task, model and harness match those behind the reported figures.
quote: In a new toy experiment, a team of 1,000 agents running an early version of Claude Fable 5.2 reproduced the proof without the scaffolding provided by Prove2Me or steering from a researcher. The team took 28.7 hours, used one-third as many output tokens, and wrote a proof one-seventh the length of the original.

claim: The only team structure Anthropic gave its 1,000-agent Fable 5.2 proof run was a hierarchy with one lead and 999 helpers.
why: The prompt told the lead to divide and assign the work and told helpers to ask the lead about unclear tasks.
check: Check which roles the harness assigns and which coordination rules the agents must work out.
quote: The only structure we gave the team was a hierarchy, consisting of one lead and 999 helpers.

claim: The team coordinated through a shared Postgres database reached from the shell, chosen because SQL offers general primitives, its transactions handle concurrent writes from 1,000 agents, and Claude is already familiar with it; work reached main only via per-agent branches and merge requests.
why: Agents had no dedicated messaging tools and used the database to claim tasks, share notes and log finished work after earlier attempts at the original formalization lost track of project state.
check: For comparable concurrent teams, check whether the shared store can handle simultaneous writes and lets agents see claims and finished work.
quote: We chose SQL because it offers general primitives for organizing information, its transactions handle concurrent writes from 1,000 agents, and Claude is already familiar with it.

claim: In the Fable 5.2 proof run, helpers initially judged 47 of the 60 statements infeasible within budget, yet the team proved most of them, leading the authors to suggest human encouragement when agents may stop too early.
why: The Langlands-Tunnell captain estimated under 1% chance of finishing in time, and the statement was proved at hour 28.4.
check: When a long-running proof team proposes dropping a statement as infeasible, check its actual progress and throughput before accepting its initial estimate as a reason to stop.
quote: Agents tend to give up on hard problems and misjudge their difficulty. Early on, helpers judged 47 of the 60 statements infeasible within the run’s budget, yet the team went on to prove most of them. Human encouragement at such moments can keep agents from stopping too early.

claim: A single shared machine hit its limits at about 100 agents, with more than half of the 100-agent runs stopped or restarted because memory, disk or CPU ran out, so the 1,000-agent run gave each agent its own lightweight virtual machine.
why: The shared-host runs were stopped or restarted when memory, disk or CPU ran out.
check: Check the number of concurrent agents against host resources and isolation.
quote: For this run, each agent had a sandbox on its own lightweight virtual machine. A single shared machine hit its limits at about 100 agents: more than half of our 100-agent runs had to be stopped or restarted because memory, disk, or CPU ran out.

claim: The post describes a real-time monitoring policy that stops the whole team for human review after a blocked tool call, while the Fable 5.2 proof run used only the action-based monitor and was configured to end on a lead block or remove just the affected helper on a helper block.
why: The team-wide stop is intended to prevent another agent from carrying out a blocked action, and monitors given chain of thought and interagent communication detected all sabotage attempts in the authors' evaluations.
check: For unattended multi-agent runs, check for sandboxing, a per-tool-call monitor and a defined stop-and-review path.
quote: In the run in this post, we used only the action-based monitor. Only a block on the lead would have ended the run; a block on a helper removed just that helper.

claim: During the 28.7-hour run the harness sent the lead 19 automatic reminders of how much time remained, each encouraging it to keep going.
why: The reminders were one way the harness explicitly encouraged the lead to persist during the run.
check: If a comparable long run uses time reminders to sustain progress, check whether the lead actually receives the remaining time and a prompt to continue.
quote: the harness sent the lead 19 automatic reminders of how much time remained, each encouraging the lead to keep going.

claim: A scheduled agent should read each source from a bookmark (the timestamp of the newest item read, stored in a memory file) rather than a fixed window such as the last 24 hours, because a late run leaves a gap and an early run repeats items.
why: The bookmark lets the window stretch or shrink to cover everything since the last run.
check: Check whether a scheduled brief uses a fixed lookback to capture everything since the last run, which can leave gaps or repeat items when the interval changes.
quote: A common mistake is asking the agent to read a fixed window like "the last 24 hours." A late run leaves a gap and an early run repeats items. Instead, give the agent a bookmark per source.

claim: In the Managed Agents brief, a run still starts without an unavailable or expired-token MCP server's tools, so the reference instructions tell it to keep that source's bookmark, report from other sources and name what it could not read.
why: A session error can leave the agent with no results from a failed source and lead it to report a quiet day.
check: Check unattended agent instructions for what to do when a source is unavailable; silence treated as no news is a finding.
quote: If an MCP server is down or its token has expired, the run still starts, just without that server's tools. The session logs an error, but the agent sees nothing from that source and reports "nothing new."

claim: The daily Slack brief checks for today's edition before posting, counts it as sent only when Slack returns `ok: true` and a message timestamp, updates its ledger and bookmarks after confirmation, and records `maybe posted` if the result is unclear.
why: Recording a post that never landed means those items are never reported; re-posting when unsure sends duplicates.
check: For a scheduled Slack brief, check that it looks for an existing edition before sending and leaves bookmarks and the ledger untouched until Slack confirms the post.
quote: First, the agent looks for today's title in the channel's recent messages and doesn't post if the edition is already there. Second, the post counts as sent only if Slack returns "ok": true and a message ts. Third, the agent updates the ledger and bookmarks only after that confirmation. If the result is unclear, it marks the run "maybe posted" and changes nothing else, so nothing is lost.

claim: The reference daily brief rechecks the live source for each planned item just before posting, drops resolved or unconfirmable items, updates text for still-open items that changed, and records unconfirmable items in the run record.
why: Items can change between reading and posting, and the reference brief treats one stale status line as more costly to trust than ten missing items.
check: For a brief that reports live status, check whether it rechecks each planned item immediately before posting and drops anything it cannot confirm.
quote: For every item you will report, re-check its live source just before posting: resolved since you read it, drop it; still open but changed, fix the line; cannot confirm, drop it and list it in the run record's cuts.

claim: For a Claude Managed Agents deployment, the post recommends starting the `deployment.md` per-run budget at three to five times the normal run cost and refining it from measurements, with runs that reach the cap pausing at `budget_reached`.
why: The cap limits runaway cost on a background schedule, but a cap set too low can make the brief appear to have gone quiet.
check: For a Managed Agents deployment, check whether its cap reflects measured run costs and whether monitoring distinguishes a `budget_reached` pause from a quiet brief.
quote: Start at three to five times the cost of a normal run, then tighten it as you see real numbers. A run that hits its cap pauses instead of failing, so a cap set too low looks like a brief that went quiet. The cap is the budget in deployment.md. Every run gets the full amount, and a run that reaches it pauses with a budget_reached stop reason:

claim: In an unattended Managed Agents run MCP tools ask for approval by default and nobody is there to give it, so the reference sets the GitHub toolset to always_allow and keeps the GitHub token read-only.
why: Text read from messages and issues can be interpreted as instructions, and a read-only GitHub token means that token cannot write to GitHub.
check: For an unattended Managed Agents brief, check whether the GitHub toolset can read without waiting for approval and whether its token is read-only.
quote: MCP tools ask for approval by default and nobody is there to give it, so the GitHub toolset is set to always_allow and the GitHub token is read-only.

claim: For user preferences that can change between scheduled runs, the daily brief rereads them at the start of each run from a store the agent cannot edit and stops with an explanation if it cannot read them.
why: A prompt copy of the preferences can keep applying rules the user has already changed.
check: Check whether the scheduled brief reads the current user preferences or relies on a prompt copy that can continue applying superseded rules.
quote: A common problem occurs when a copy of the preferences is baked into the prompt, which keeps applying rules you've already changed. Have the agent read the file fresh every run. If it can't read the file, it should stop and say so instead of running on defaults.

claim: Anthropic's single-agent-loop kit does not assume one loop always wins: every change is scored on the same eval before and after, and a subagent is removed only when the numbers show its replacement holds, with a verdict of fold, merge, call as a tool or keep for each subagent.
why: The kit treats a scored comparison as the evidence for a migration decision, and its published real-model evidence is limited to two runs of one example by one person.
check: When folding, merging or replacing a subagent in a migration toward one loop, check whether the change is scored before and after on the same eval.
quote:
Every change is scored on
the same eval before and after, and a subagent only goes away when the numbers say its
replacement holds.

claim: The kit lists three reasons to keep a subagent: parallel research across fresh contexts, independent verification, and work that reads far more than the main agent needs afterwards.
why: Each of these earns its own context, whereas subagents that always run together should be merged and others folded into skills and tools or called as tools with a structured result.
check: Classify each subagent against these three reasons; one that fits none, or that always runs with another, is a fold or merge candidate.
quote:
Parallel research across fresh contexts,
  independent verification, or work that reads far more than the main agent needs
  afterwards are good reasons to keep a subagent.

claim: The kit's `chain_coverage.py` checks that the eval has a task for every chain of subagents production uses, so regressions in a handoff can be tested after a fold.
why: An eval that covers only single-agent paths can pass while a multi-hop handoff quietly regresses.
check: Check that the eval exercises every handoff chain in the real system, not only the common one.
quote: Checks the eval has a task for every chain of subagents production uses, so a dropped handoff cannot go unseen

claim: The kit's reference loop requires a write gate when a tool writes, counts subagent tokens against the budget, caps a batch of tool calls and, when its optional verifier rejects an answer twice, withholds it.
why: The README says these changes were checked offline after the two real-model runs.
check: Check that a verifier loop has a defined number of rejections after which output is withheld or escalated, rather than looping or shipping the rejected answer.
quote:
a write gate is required when a tool writes, subagent tokens count
  against the budget, a batch of tool calls is capped, and an answer the verifier rejects
  twice is withheld.

claim: A Claude Code system-prompt change shipped alongside Opus 4.7 on April 16 capped text between tool calls at 25 words and final replies at 100 words, except for final replies on tasks that required more detail.
why: Anthropic introduced the limits to reduce verbosity after weeks of internal testing showed no regressions on the evals it ran.
check: If a workflow copied the April 16 prompt, check what it caps between tool calls and whether the final-reply cap allows for tasks that need more detail.
quote:
“Length limits: keep text between tool calls to ≤25 words. Keep final responses to ≤100 words unless the task requires more detail.”
After multiple weeks of internal testing and no regressions in the set of evaluations we ran, we felt confident about the change and shipped it alongside Opus 4.7 on April 16.

claim: Anthropic added guidance to its `CLAUDE.md` to gate model-specific Claude Code system prompt changes to the model they target.
why: Claude Code tunes its system prompt for models that can behave differently from one another.
check: Check whether a prompt change intended for one model is gated so it only applies to that model.
quote: We've additionally added guidance to our CLAUDE.md to ensure model-specific changes are gated to the specific model they're targeting.

claim: Anthropic said it would add soak periods, broader evals, and gradual rollouts for Claude Code system prompt changes that could reduce intelligence.
why: The extra controls were meant to catch intelligence regressions earlier.
check: For a prompt change that could reduce intelligence, check for soak time, expanded eval coverage, and a staged rollout.
quote: For any change that could trade off against intelligence, we'll add soak periods, a broader eval suite, and gradual rollouts so we catch issues earlier.

claim: In a Claude Code study with Opus 4.8 at High effort, 77% of post-task survey respondents repeated an agent argument in at least one answer and 15% credited the agent anywhere.
why: Respondents explained their choices without access to their agent conversations.
check: For agent-assisted decisions, check whether the decision record credits arguments drawn from the agent.
quote: Analysts couldn’t look back at their conversations with the agent while answering. Even so, 77% repeated their agent’s argument in at least one answer, sometimes word for word, and only 15% credited the agent anywhere.

claim: A verification subagent can still help when the orchestrator is less capable, verification needs specialized tools, or the workflow calls for explicit verification checkpoints.
why: A verifier can test the artifact with little context about how the main agent built it.
check: Before removing a verifier, check whether it covers work the orchestrator cannot assess reliably, uses specialized tools, or enforces a required checkpoint.
quote: verification subagents remain valuable when using less capable orchestrators, when verification requires specialized tools, or when you want to enforce explicit verification checkpoints in your workflow.

claim: The September Fermat's Last Theorem formalization, the baseline for the Fable 5.2 run, took 11 days and roughly 6 billion output tokens with dozens of agents on an internal model roughly comparable to Claude Fable 5.1.
why: The September team relied on Prove2Me and researcher direction, both of which the Fable 5.2 run omitted.
check: When using the September figures as a baseline, check whether the comparison accounts for differences in the model, team size, and scaffolding.
quote: Our September formalization took a researcher and dozens of agents 11 days and roughly 6 billion output tokens.

claim: The lead in the Fable 5.2 proof run set up five shared database tables in the first 10 minutes to coordinate the team.
why: The tables gave agents shared places for orders, assignments, notes, subtasks, and finished work.
check: If agents must set up their own coordination, check whether they have a shared store for assignments, progress, and completed work.
quote: In the first 10 minutes, the lead set up five shared database tables to coordinate the team. The lead wrote orders and assignments, helpers logged finished work and managed the subtasks table, and both wrote to the notes table.

claim: During the Fable 5.2 proof run, the lead let free helpers pick up work on other statements without waiting for an assignment.
why: Helpers also began adding and claiming subtasks as they took on more responsibility for solving each statement.
check: Check whether available helpers can claim work when waiting for an individual assignment would leave them idle.
quote: At first, the lead also assigned helpers to specific statements. This started to change within the first hour, and by the third hour, the lead told the free helpers, “do not wait for me.” This let free helpers pick up work on different statements without waiting for the lead, even as it kept writing new assignments.

claim: Anthropic said it would keep ablating individual lines of the Claude Code system prompt to measure what each line changes.
why: A broader ablation surfaced an eval drop from a verbosity instruction that passed the initial internal evals.
check: Check whether prompt evals compare versions that differ by just the line under review.
quote: We will run a broad suite of per-model evals for every system prompt change to Claude Code, continuing ablations to understand the impact of each line
